abstract: The ability of the plant hormone auxin to stimulate growth by promoting cell expansion has fascinated biologists for more than a century and provided the bioassay that ultimately led to auxin's chemical identification as indole-3-acetic acid (IAA). In the early 1970s, the acid growth theory of auxin-induced cell expansion was proposed. This model posited that auxin promotes H+ efflux into the apoplast, lowering cell wall pH to activate wall-loosening processes while also hyperpolarizing the plasma membrane, thereby promoting solute transport to support the hydraulic conditions required for expansion. Although supported by a wealth of creative physiological experiments, the theory initially lacked substantial genetic support and defined mechanisms linking auxin perception to proton pump activation. Over the past two decades, advances in genetics, cell biology, and biomechanics have transformed this classical theory into a broader, context-dependent framework in which auxin signaling regulates plasma membrane H⁺-ATPases, ion and water transport, and cell wall remodeling. Importantly, auxin does not invariably acidify the apoplast or promote elongation: roots provide a prominent counterexample in which rapid auxin signaling can drive surface alkalinization, membrane depolarization, and growth inhibition. To celebrate the centennial of Plant Physiology, we highlight three seminal papers published in the journal that were instrumental in laying the foundations of the acid growth model, and examine how subsequent discoveries have revitalized and expanded the concept into an integrated signaling-mechanics framework for understanding plant cell expansion.
